newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan erases some bond mkt tightening doubts.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan erases some bond mkt tightening doubts.

text.p: If there was any doubt in the U.S. Treasury market that the Federal Reserve would leave rates alone at Tuesday's meeting, it was virtually taken out on Thursday morning after more hawkish comments from Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan.

Greenspan, in testimony before Congress's Joint Economic Committee, spoke of an economy with a great deal of vigor, with a strong job market. He stressed the Fed's need to act pre-emptively on inflation, and that any effect from tighter monetary policy in the near-term would not be felt for a while.

Greenspan "confirmed the market's worst fears," said Kevin Sluder, head trader at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc, adding that he believes the tightening odds are now 95 percent, from 60 percent before Greenspan's remarks.

Consequently, Treasury yields across the curve jumped, with bill rates up as much as six basis points, the two-year note's yield rising as high as 6.27 percent and the 30-year bond's yield up to 7.01 percent -- levels seen as about fully priced for a rate hike.

The long end moved into positive territory as the day wore on, with the bond's yield falling back to 6.98 percent. Long-end investors cheered Greenspan's comments in noting the Fed's vigilance at keeping inflation at bay. Yet, the short end continued to remain depressed -- evidenced by interest rate sensitive bill rates which were up as much as five basis points.

"Most people are now saying there's little doubt left and very little chance that they don't do anything," Sluder said. "(Greenspan) certainly re-emphasized and reclarified the Fed's resolve and a lot of people were swayed by what he said."

According to the latest Reuters poll released on Thursday, 34 of 48 U.S. firms are currently calling for a March 25 rate hike. Of the 34, six economists moved into the rate hike camp after reviewing Greenspan's comments.

It has taken a considerable amount of time for market participants to collectively get on the same page on Fed action. But some noted that there may still be some more room for Treasury yields at the short end to rise.
Bill rates could rise another 10 basis points, while the two-year note is seen backing up to about 6.30 percent, they said.
"If funds are going to 5.5 percent and then to 5.75 percent, do you want to be be an aggressive buyer here?" Zions First National Bank bill trader Richard Schwarz asked rhetorically.

Should the Fed confirm the market's view and tighten, players said the two-year note should trade up to about a 6.40 percent yield and the 30-year bond to 7.05 percent -- a substantial narrowing of the yield curve. And it is likely the market will start to price in another move at the Fed's May or July meeting.

"The front end has further (back up) to go," said Michelle Colley Laughlin, chief U.S. Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc. "The long end will have a negative reaction but the back end is more appropriately priced (for a tightening)."
A minority, however, still does not believe the Fed will move at this time.
Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Securities Co, said after seeing the initial Greenspan headlines, he became convinced that a 25 basis point hike was a done deal.
But after reading the text of Greenspan's testimony, he said he would leave his forecast of no Fed move until May intact since the Fed chief noted that inflation is not a problem right now.
Greenspan "wants to (raise rates) but he is not certain that the balance of risks and rewards justify a move right now," he said.
